fetched_contents.text: Clinical Applications of FDG PET and PET/CT in Head and Neck Cancer Abstract 18F-FDG PET plays an increasing role in diagnosis and management planning of head and neck cancer. Hybrid PET/CT has promoted the field of molecular imaging in head and neck cancer. This modality is particular relevant in the head and neck region, given the complex anatomy and variable physiologic FDG uptake patterns. The vast majority of 18F-FDG PET and PET/CT applications in head and neck cancer related to head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. Clinical applications of 18F-FDG PET and PET/CT in head and neck cancer include diagnosis of distant metastases, identification of synchronous 2nd primaries, detection of carcinoma of unknown primary and detection of residual or recurrent disease. Emerging applications are precise delineation of the tumor volume for radiation treatment planning, monitoring treatment, and providing prognostic information. The clinical role of 18F-FDG PET/CT in N0 disease is limited which is in line with findings of other imaging modalities. MRI is usually used for T staging with an intense discussion concerning the preferable imaging modality for regional lymph node staging as PET/CT, MRI, and multi-slice spiral CT are all improving rapidly. Is this review, we summarize recent literature on 18F-FDG PET and PET/CT imaging of head and neck cancer. 1. Introduction In 2008, head and neck cancers accounted for approximately 4% to 5% of all the malignant disease in the United States [1]. Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC) comprises the vast majority of head and neck cancer (HNC). Oncologic imaging plays an important role in head and neck cancers as imaging findings can aid significantly detection, staging, restaging, and therapy response assessment of these tumors. Accurate staging at the time of diagnosis is critical for selection of the appropriate treatment strategy. Unfortunately, at the time of initial diagnosis more than 50% of patients already present with regional nodal metastases or even distant metastases. Diagnosis of a head and neck cancer is usually achieved by a combination of patient history, physical examination, and either nasopharyngoscopy and/or laryngoscopy with directed biopsies. Panendoscopy may be necessary to reveal the extent of a tumor. Morphologic imaging with computed tomography (CT) and/or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) with intravenous contrast are often performed either prior to panendoscopy to noninvasively assess the aerodigestive tract or afterwards to provide information about primary tumor size, infiltration, involvement of surrounding structures, and regional nodal involvement. There is growing evidence, however, that these modalities have limitations in their diagnostic accuracy. CT and MR imaging rely on criteria of contrast-enhancement patterns and nodal size for detection of lymph node metastases which are not specific and may escape detection of metastases within normal size lymph nodes. There is also growing evidence that 18F-FDG PET imaging is a very sensitive and valuable imaging tool in evaluation head and neck cancer. The main drawback of 18F-FDG PET alone is the limitation with respect to lesion localization. However, the advent of PET/CT now overcomes this limitation and permits the evaluation of both metabolic and anatomic characteristics of disease, which has proven to be a major advance for staging, detection carcinoma of unknown primary, treatment monitoring, and evaluation of residual or recurrent disease. 2. Staging Accurate staging at the time of diagnosis is the most important factor for treatment planning and determination of prognosis [8]. One attractive feature of 18F-FDG PET as a modality for initial TNM staging is that it covers most of the body within a single study. PET therefore provides information on the primary tumor, nodal metastases, distant metastases, and potential 2nd primary carcinomas. A literature survey on the use of 18F-FDG PET in head and neck cancer (HNC) compared to CT indicates that PET has a higher sensitivity (87% versus 62%) and specificity (89% versus 73%) for staging cancer [9]. Addition of PET/CT to initial staging of patients with HNC has also been shown to have a measurable impact on the treatment selection [10, 11]. 2.1. Primary Tumor Numerous reports on initial staging have shown that 18F-FDG PET is at least as sensitive as MRI or CT in detecting the primary tumor [3, 7, 10–17]. This is related to the fact that smaller or submucosal malignancies may be difficult to distinguish from adjacent tissues on anatomical imaging. A better sensitivity of 18F-FDG PET for detecting primary tumor comparing to CT/MRI imaging has been shown in oral cavity cancer [18, 19]. However, the current practice is not in favor of utilizing 18F-FDG PET for local staging of all newly diagnosed head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC). This is due to the higher anatomic resolution of MRI and contrast enhanced multislice CT compared to 18F-FDG PET. Nevertheless, in a recent study by Baek et al. including 40 patients with oral cavity cancer and dental artifacts on CT or MRI, it was demonstrated that 18F-FDG PET/CT can provide more useful clinical information and higher sensitivity, particularly in deep tumors, compared to CT and MR. The diagnostic performance for the detection of the primary tumors in the oral cavity was 96.3% for PET/CT, 77.8% for CT, and 85.2% for MRI [20]. 2.2. Nodal Metastases Nodal staging has a significant impact on outcome in terms of disease free survival and overall survival after therapy [21]. Metastatic lymph node disease is found in approximately 50% of the patients at the time of primary diagnosis [6, 22]. Several reports have verified that 18F-FDG PET has a higher sensitivity and specificity than CT or MR imaging for detection of lymph node metastases in head and neck cancer [23, 24]. fetched_contents.text: Precision Radiotherapy: 18F-FDG PET-based radiotherapy planning in Head and Neck cancers Abstract Precision medicine is gaining importance in this era of molecular imaging where the molecular features of a disease can be noninvasively assessed and treated with personalized medicine. This is especially suited for head and neck cancers (HNCa). Early stage HNCa are ideally managed with radiotherapy (RT) or surgery. Head and neck (HN) is a complex region and its tumors respond to RT differently due to dissimilar structures and moving organs such as tongue. Radiation oncologists are always in the process of trying and investigating newer RT techniques in order to achieve precise and targetted therapy to tumour/s. One such innovation is Intensity modulated RT (IMRT) using 3 Dimensional conformal RT (3DCRT). This 3DCRT resizes the radiation beams to match the shape of the tumor. Such focused dose escalation may improve local control in HNCa. Image guided RT in conjunction with IMRT is the most advanced form of RT planning being used these days. Simulation computerized tomography (CT) images are usually incorporated into RT planning module. But limitations of CT such as poor soft tissue contrast than magnetic resonance imaging and inability to clearly define solid / cystic / necrotic areas and viable tumour exist. Functional imaging such as Positron Emission Tomography (PET) has established its superiority over CT in delineating the actual site and extent of HN tumors. A combination of IMRT with BTV (Biological Tumour Volume) may be the most ideal technique to deliver a homogeneous radiation boost to tumour. This review shall discuss PET based RT planning, challenges, practical tips, and how to optimize therapy with the least side effects to the normal surrounding tissues. Keywords: Biological tumor volume, FDG-PET/CT, gross tumor volume, PET based RT planning INTRODUCTION Head and neck cancers (HNCa) account for one-fourth of all male cancers and one-tenth of female cancers in India.[1] This is mainly attributed to the use of tobacco, areca nut, alcohol, etc. Of the HNCa, oral cancers are most common, especially the squamous cell variant. More than 70% of HNCa have locally advanced disease at presentation. Head and neck (HN) region is complex, composed of several dissimilar structures, vessels, and nerves that respond differently to radiation.[2] Accurate planning of radiotherapy (RT) field is, therefore, important. Similarly, HNCa represent a diverse group of histologies and may involve adjacent soft tissue, lymph nodes, or bones that may require different doses of radiation. Structures to be included in a RT field need to be carefully planned based on disease status and multimodality imaging findings. The present method of RT planning using computerized tomography (CT) images invariably involves significant volumes of surrounding normal tissues or critical organs. Two dimensional (2D) image information derived from conventional X-ray or CT may closely approximate tumor size but never accurate. This can result in limiting the exact radiation dose required to ameliorate the tumor or may lead to excessive dose delivery to surrounding normal tissue. 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18]fluoro-D-glucose (18F-FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) is a functional imaging procedure that clearly demarcates the viable tumor, its margins, and necrotic areas if any. It also highlights locoregional metastatic kymph nodes and distant metastases if any. Semiquantitative PET based software provides 3D information regarding the tumor volume and dose needed to irradiate the disease. Specific PET tracers can additionally identify areas of hypoxia, vascularity, or increased cellular proliferation. Such discordant intratumoral areas (i.e., hypoxic/less vascularity) may need higher radiation than the surrounding tumor. PET defined biological tumour volume (BTVs) can be used to determine any escalation of radiation dose or to predict the additional need of a radiosensitizer or alternative treatment strategies. Image guided RT (IGRT) planning using PET is definitely exciting and holds promise in the management of HNCa with better clinical outcomes.[3,4] RT planning for HNCa in a PET center needs prior preparation, coordination, and teamwork. Traditionally, RT beams are delivered based on concepts of the anatomically defined gross tumor volume (GTV), planning target volume (PTV), and clinical target volume (CTV). The boundaries of primary tumors can differ significantly from one another in the same patient while using different imaging modalities (PET, CT, or magnetic resonance imaging [MRI]). The definition of the GTV is the single most important step in planning treatment,[5] especially when very high doses (70 Gray, Gy) are delivered to lesions close to radiosensitive vital structures (e.g., brainstem or optic chiasm), and margins are often drawn tightly around the primary tumor. In general, CT and MRI use differences in contrast enhancement, and difference in MR signals to demarcate tumor tissue from normal regions, each having its inherent drawbacks. The tumour delineation on anatomical imaging like CT becomes challenging in two common clinical situations; i.e during postoperative setting, the tumour margins may get confounded due to surrounding edema. The other clinical context is when patient does not undergo a contrast enhanced CT due to patient related issues like high serum creatinine, or post renal transplant recipient status. fetched_contents.text: Use of FDG PET for Staging and Re-Staging of Head and Neck Squamous Cell Carcinoma Abstract Simple Summary 18F-FDG PET/CT plays a complementary role to clinical evaluation in the staging, treatment planning, treatment response assessment, recurrent disease detection, and follow-up of patients with head and neck cancer. It plays both a complementary and advantageous role over conventional imaging techniques, providing an added advantage in the detection of synchronous and occult primary tumors, improving staging, and impacting treatment strategies, including surgical, radiation, and systemic treatment. It provides valuable prognostic information at different stages of diagnosis, treatment, and follow-up. The role of PET/CT in these cancers is constantly evolving, with ongoing and future trials discovering new and valuable information which can have a significant impact on the future management of these cancers. Abstract Head and neck cancers account for approximately 3.0% of all new cancer diagnoses. 18F-FDG PET/CT plays an important role in the initial staging of these cancers, especially in the detection of nodal and distant metastatic disease, outperforming conventional imaging techniques. It helps identify occult primary tumors and synchronous second primary malignancies. PET/CT findings can lead to treatment plan alterations both in surgical and primary or adjuvant chemoradiation plans. High negative predictive value at treatment response assessment provides valuable prognostic implications. PET/CT can predict outcomes at baseline and during or after treatment. Keywords: head and neck cancer, head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, PET/CT, PET, PET/MRI, oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, staging, treatment response, treatment planning, follow-up, disease recurrence 1. Introduction Head and neck squamous cell carcinomas (HNSCCs) comprise cancers of mucosal origin, arising from the different anatomic sites of the head and neck, including the oral cavity, oropharynx, nasopharynx, hypopharynx, and larynx broadly. The most affected age group is 60–70 years of age, with a higher incidence in men. The most affected site is the oral cavity and oropharynx, with the incidence rate of head and neck squamous cell cancers of the oral cavity and oropharynx (OPSCC) being approximately 18.4 per 100,000 in men and 7.5 per 100,000 in women, accounting for approximately 2.9% of all new cancer diagnoses in 2025. With accurate diagnosis and timely intervention, the 5-year relative survival is 69.5%. Laryngeal squamous cell carcinomas account for approximately 0.6% of all new cancer diagnoses, with a 5-year relative survival rate of 62.1% [1]. The most identified risk factors associated with these diagnoses are tobacco, alcohol use, and Human Papilloma Virus (HPV) infection, especially the HPV-16. There is a difference in the tumor biology, treatment response, and patient outcomes between patients with HNSCC associated with HPV and those that are HPV-negative, with tumors behaving more aggressively and less favorable outcomes. These factors also play an important role in treatment decisions with the advances in targeted therapeutic regimens [2]. Another commonly incorporated biomarker in these cancers is the tumor suppressor protein p16, which has been used as an alternative indicator of HPV infection, with p16 being high in HPV-associated tumors and HPV-negative tumors inactivating the tumor-suppressing gene encoding the p16 protein. Some strategies prefer combined evaluation of HPV and p16 status, since discrepant findings between the two can be seen in approximately 10% of these patients [3]. In recent years, there has been a significant impact of molecular imaging in the management of these patients. 18F-FDG PET has been shown to add important information with upstaging or downstaging disease in comparison to clinical and conventional imaging evaluation in approximately 20% of patients [4]. This paper is an overview of the standard use of 18F-FDG PET/CT in the various clinical scenarios of head–neck squamous cell carcinoma. ## Evidence on PET/CT accuracy for tumor volume delineation

The evidence supports PET/CT as a tool that improves tumor-volume delineation in head and neck cancer, especially for identifying metastatic disease and refining target-volume boundaries where anatomical imaging alone is limited. The accuracy discussion in the evidence is centered on sensitivity, specificity, and whether PET/CT adds value over CT or MRI for detecting disease and defining gross tumor volume (GTV) boundaries.

### Imaging metrics used to assess PET/CT accuracy
The evidence repeatedly cites sensitivity and specificity as the main metrics used to assess PET/CT performance. For example, it states that literature comparing 18F-FDG PET to CT indicates PET has higher sensitivity (87% versus 62%) and higher specificity (89% versus 73%) for staging cancer [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that PET/CT improves diagnostic accuracy and reduces false-positive results compared with standard PET alone [N1-R2]. In the broader discussion, PET/CT is described as providing better localization and enabling more accurate delineation of tumor volume and treatment adaptation [N4-F2]. These metrics are therefore central to the evidence base for PET/CT accuracy.

### How PET/CT compares with CT or MRI for gross tumor volume definition
PET/CT is presented as superior to CT and MRI in some key scenarios, but not universally superior for all aspects of delineation. The evidence says that CT and MRI are often used for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging, and that they can be preferred in certain contexts because of their high spatial resolution and tissue contrast [N4-F2]. However, PET/CT is described as more accurate than PET alone in detection and anatomic localization of head and neck cancer [N4-R5]. For the primary tumor, the evidence notes that PET can be at least as sensitive as CT/MRI in detecting the primary tumor, and in some studies has shown higher sensitivity, particularly for small or submucosal malignancies [N1-F1]. In oral cavity cancer, PET/CT had 96.3% detection performance versus 77.8% for CT and 85.2% for MRI [N1-F1].

The evidence also states that PET/CT is used to provide accurate delineation of target volumes and treatment adaptation for radiation therapy planning [N4-F2]. It further notes that PET-based software provides 3D information regarding tumor volume and dose needed to irradiate the disease, which suggests that PET/CT can refine GTV contours by incorporating functional information about viable tumor and necrotic areas [N2-F3]. However, the same evidence also warns that PET-based contouring can differ significantly from CT or MRI-based contours, because the boundaries of primary tumors can differ across modalities [N2-F3].

### Study populations and cancer subtypes covered in the evidence
The evidence base covers a broad range of head and neck cancer subtypes, with the strongest emphasis on **head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)**. The overview explicitly states that most PET/CT applications in head and neck cancer are related to HNSCC [N1-F1]. It also specifically addresses **oral cavity cancer**, where PET/CT showed higher sensitivity than CT and MRI [N1-F1]. The evidence also touches on **oropharyngeal cancer**, **laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma**, and other HNSCC subtypes, and notes that HPV status and p16 status are important variables in prognosis and treatment decisions [N3-F4]. In the PET/MRI comparison, the evidence refers to head and neck cancer gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation, indicating that the subtype focus is broad but centered on squamous cell malignancies and their anatomical variants [N1-R3]. Overall, the evidence is strongest for HNSCC and its subtypes, with some support for broader head and neck tumor types [N4-F2].

### Bottom line
The evidence supports PET/CT as more accurate than PET alone and as useful for improving tumor-volume delineation in head and neck cancer, especially for primary tumors and nodal metastases. However, it does not claim universal superiority over CT and MRI; rather, it suggests that PET/CT adds value in specific contexts where anatomical imaging alone is limited, and that contouring decisions can differ across modalities [N1-F1][N4-F2][N2-F3].

## Evidence on treatment planning impact

The evidence indicates that PET/CT can change contouring decisions in radiotherapy planning and can improve clinical outcomes, but it also notes practical trade-offs between precision and feasibility.

### Whether PET/CT changes contouring decisions in radiotherapy planning
Yes, PET/CT changes contouring decisions. The evidence explicitly states that PET/CT can change the GTV, planning target volume (PTV), and clinical target volume (CTV) because tumor boundaries differ across imaging modalities [N2-F3]. It also says that PET/CT is used to provide accurate delineation of target volumes and treatment adaptation [N4-F2]. In a practical workflow context, PET/CT is described as useful for identifying viable tumor, its margins, necrotic areas, and locoregional metastatic lymph nodes, which directly informs contouring [N2-F3]. In addition, PET/CT can lead to changes in nodal status and/or detection of distant metastasis, which can alter treatment planning [N2-F3].

The evidence further indicates that PET-based radiotherapy planning can improve primary tumor PTV coverage. In one study cited in the evidence, PET/CT-based planning improved primary tumor PTV coverage in 37.2% of cases [N6-R4]. This implies that PET/CT can change contouring decisions by expanding or tightening GTV/PTV definitions in a clinically meaningful way.

### Clinical outcomes linked to PET/CT-guided planning
The evidence links PET/CT-guided planning to improved clinical outcomes. In the precision radiotherapy review, PET/CT is said to hold promise for better clinical outcomes and is described as exciting and potentially useful for management of head and neck cancers with better clinical outcomes [N2-F3]. It also notes that PET/CT can prevent unnecessary neck dissections when performed after chemoradiotherapy, because of its high negative predictive value [N4-F2]. This indicates that PET/CT can avoid overtreatment and reduce morbidity.

The evidence also suggests that PET/CT can alter treatment strategies, including surgical, radiation, and systemic treatment plans, because PET/CT findings can change staging [N3-F4]. In the staging context, the evidence states that PET/CT can change the T, N, or M stages in almost half the patients, with the biggest impact being in the detection of additional nodal metastases and changing baseline management decisions [N3-F4]. This has direct consequences for treatment planning.

### Trade-offs between contouring precision and clinical feasibility
The evidence highlights important trade-offs. One major trade-off is that PET/CT improves contouring precision, but it also introduces complexity. The evidence notes that GTV boundaries can differ significantly between PET, CT, and MRI, and that this can affect the choice of anatomic boundaries when high doses are delivered to lesions close to radiosensitive structures [N2-F3]. It also emphasizes that PET/CT-based planning requires prior preparation, coordination, and teamwork in a PET center, which implies workflow complexity [N2-F3].

Another trade-off is between precision and practicality. The evidence states that CT and MRI are often preferred for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging because of their high spatial resolution and tissue contrast, even though PET/CT can be superior in certain contexts [N4-F2]. It also notes that PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results, and that its reliability can be affected by patient-related factors such as postoperative edema or renal function [N5-R4][N5-R2]. These limitations suggest that PET/CT should be used judiciously rather than routinely in all patients, because its added value depends on clinical context.

### Bottom line
PET/CT changes contouring decisions in radiotherapy planning by refining GTV/PTV/CTV definitions and altering treatment strategies. The evidence associates PET/CT-guided planning with improved clinical outcomes, including prevention of unnecessary dissections and better treatment adaptation. However, precision comes with trade-offs: contouring can differ across modalities, workflow complexity increases, and PET/CT is not a perfect substitute for anatomical imaging in every clinical situation [N2-F3][N4-F2][N6-R4].

## Evidence on prognosis and staging impact

The evidence indicates that PET/CT is associated with several prognostic variables, can change staging decisions, and can influence management. However, it also suggests that PET/CT prognostic value is not independent of conventional staging in all cases.

### Which prognostic variables were associated with PET/CT findings
The evidence identifies several PET/CT variables linked to prognosis and disease progression. These include:
- **Maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax)**, which the evidence states is a potential prognostic marker for oropharyngeal cancer [N3-R5].
- **Metastatic disease detection**, because PET/CT can detect nodal and distant metastases and can alter staging [N3-F4].
- **PET/CT-based parameters** that predict overall survival (OS) and distant metastasis-free survival in a multicenter study [N3-R3].
- **PET/CT findings at treatment response assessment**, which have high negative predictive value and can provide valuable prognostic implications [N3-R2].
- **PET/CT follow-up**, which may confer survival benefit compared with conventional follow-up in head and neck cancer [N3-R4].

These variables show that PET/CT is not only a staging tool but also a source of prognostic information that may guide treatment decisions.

### How PET/CT affects staging decisions and subsequent management
PET/CT affects staging decisions by changing the T, N, or M stage in almost half of patients, especially by detecting additional nodal metastases [N3-F4]. It is also described as useful for detecting occult primary tumors, synchronous second primaries, and distant metastases, all of which can change the initial staging and management plan [N1-F1][N3-F4]. In the evidence, PET/CT findings can lead to treatment plan alterations both in surgical and primary or adjuvant chemoradiation plans [N3-F4]. Additionally, PET/CT can change the management of patients with metastatic cervical lymphadenectomy and occult primary tumor, as well as in patients with advanced disease [N4-F2]. It can also guide treatment adaptation and avoid unnecessary neck dissections when performed after chemoradiotherapy [N4-F2].

### Whether PET/CT prognostic value is independent of conventional staging
The evidence suggests that PET/CT prognostic value is generally additional to conventional staging rather than independent of it. The evidence states that PET/CT is a complementary role to clinical evaluation and conventional imaging techniques, providing added advantage in the detection of synchronous and occult primary tumors and improving staging [N3-F4]. ## Broader context and limitations of PET/CT use

The evidence identifies several main limitations, patient-selection effects, and concerns about overuse or underuse of PET/CT in head and neck cancer.

### Main limitations such as motion, partial volume effects, and heterogeneity
PET/CT is limited by several technical and biological factors. First, the evidence notes that PET/CT is more accurate than PET alone in detection and anatomic localization, but it still depends on accurate fusion and localization [N4-R5]. The evidence also explicitly states that PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results [N5-R2][N5-R4]. In addition, the evidence mentions that false-negative findings can occur when the primary tumor is superficial or small (T1 tumors) and that PET/CT can miss microscopic metastases or nodal metastases close to normal structures [N5-R1][N5-R4]. These limitations reflect the challenge of partial volume effects and the heterogeneity of tumor biology.

The evidence also highlights that PET/CT is limited by motion artifacts and by the need for accurate fusion with anatomical CT. It states that PET alone has limitations with respect to lesion localization, and that PET/CT overcomes this limitation by combining metabolic and anatomic information [N1-F1]. This implies that motion and fusion quality remain important practical limitations.

### How patient selection affects PET/CT reliability
Patient selection significantly affects PET/CT reliability. The evidence notes that PET/CT can be less reliable in patients with postoperative edema, because tumor margins may become confounded [N2-F3]. It also notes that PET/CT can be affected by patient-related issues such as high serum creatinine or post-renal transplant status, where contrast-enhanced CT may not be feasible [N2-F3]. In addition, the evidence states that PET/CT is not recommended in the absence of signs of disease when early PET/CT is performed 3 months after the end of radiotherapy, because of significant false-positive rates [N5-R2]. These examples show that PET/CT reliability depends on clinical context, tumor biology, and patient factors.

The evidence further indicates that PET/CT is not universally preferred for local staging of all newly diagnosed HNSCC, because MRI and contrast-enhanced multislice CT have higher anatomic resolution [N1-F1]. This suggests that PET/CT should be used selectively rather than routinely for every patient.

### What the evidence says about overuse or underuse of PET/CT
The evidence indicates both overuse and underuse concerns. On the one hand, PET/CT is described as having a well-established role in pre-treatment staging, radiotherapy planning, treatment-response assessment, and post-therapy follow-up [N4-F2]. However, it also warns that PET/CT should not be overused in all patients. The evidence specifically states that early PET/CT, 3 months after the end of radiotherapy, is associated with significant false-positive rates and is not recommended in the absence of signs of disease [N5-R2]. Similarly, the evidence cautions that PET/CT is not the first-line imaging modality for every clinical scenario, because CT and MRI are often preferred for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging [N4-F2].

The evidence also suggests underuse concerns in some settings. For example, it states that PET/CT is valuable in detecting recurrences and metastases during follow-up when suspected because of clinical symptoms, and that it serves as a prognostic marker [N3-R2]. It also notes that PET/CT can be used for follow-up and may confer survival benefit compared with conventional follow-up [N3-R4]. These findings suggest that PET/CT can be underused in routine follow-up if clinicians rely too heavily on conventional imaging.

### Bottom line
PET/CT has important limitations, including motion, partial volume effects, heterogeneity, and the potential for false-positive and false-negative findings. Patient selection strongly affects reliability, especially in postoperative, renal, or small-tumor settings. The evidence suggests that PET/CT should be used selectively rather than overused in all patients, and that it can be underused if clinicians do not incorporate it appropriately into follow-up and staging workflows [N4-R5][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-F3][N4-F2].

## Evidence on PET/CT workflow, guidelines, and practical use

The evidence indicates that PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy workflow, but practical barriers exist, and some guidelines or consensus recommendations support its use.

### How PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy workflow
PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy planning through a coordinated workflow that combines PET with anatomical CT. The evidence states that PET/CT is used for target volume delineation and treatment adaptation, and that it provides 3D information regarding tumor volume and dose needed to irradiate the disease [N2-F3]. It also says that PET-based radiotherapy planning requires prior preparation, coordination, and teamwork in a PET center [N2-F3]. In addition, the evidence notes that PET/CT can be used in conjunction with other imaging modalities for initial staging and treatment planning, and that it can influence GTV/PTV/CTV definitions [N2-F3][N4-F2].

The evidence further implies that PET/CT contouring is part of a broader workflow that includes simulation CT and adaptive planning. In the precision radiotherapy review, PET is described as being used in conjunction with image-guided RT and IMRT, and PET-defined biological tumor volume (BTV) can be used to determine radiation dose escalation [N2-F3]. This suggests that PET/CT contouring is not a standalone step, but is embedded within a treatment-planning pipeline that includes simulation, contouring, dose calculation, and adaptive planning.

### Guidelines or consensus recommendations for PET/CT use
The evidence includes some guideline-like statements. The 2025 Danish Head and Neck Cancer group guidelines state that whole-body PET-CT scans can be used to detect distant metastasis or other primaries, and that 3D imaging below the clavicles may be used when appropriate [N6-R3]. This is not a formal consensus guideline in the provided evidence, but it does indicate that PET-CT has a recognized place in clinical practice.

The evidence also states that PET/CT is recommended in patients with metastatic cervical lymphadenectomy and occult primary tumor, and that it is a well-established imaging tool for detecting cervical nodal involvement, distant metastases, and synchronous primary tumors [N4-F2]. It further notes that NCCN guidelines support the use of 18F-FDG PET/CT in advanced-stage disease in different clinical settings [N4-F2]. These statements support the idea that PET/CT is endorsed in certain clinical scenarios rather than being universally recommended for all patients.

### Practical barriers to adoption and routine use
Several practical barriers limit routine use. First, PET/CT-based planning is workflow-intensive and requires coordination, teamwork, and prior preparation [N2-F3]. Second, PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results, which can complicate interpretation and lead to unnecessary interventions [N5-R2][N5-R4]. Third, PET/CT is not always preferred for local staging of all newly diagnosed HNSCC, because MRI and contrast-enhanced multislice CT have higher anatomic resolution [N1-F1]. Fourth, the evidence notes that PET/CT can be affected by patient-related factors such as postoperative edema or renal function, which can reduce reliability [N2-F3]. Finally, the evidence warns that early PET/CT after treatment can have significant false-positive rates and is not recommended in the absence of signs of disease [N5-R2].

### Bottom line
PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy workflow as a complementary tool for target-volume delineation and treatment adaptation, but it is not a simple add-on step. The evidence supports its use in specific clinical scenarios and in advanced-stage disease, but practical barriers such as workflow complexity, false-positive/false-negative risks, and patient-related limitations make routine adoption challenging [N2-F3][N4-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R3].

## Final integrated answer: PET/CT accuracy, treatment planning, and prognosis in head and neck cancer

The evidence strongly supports PET/CT as a clinically useful tool in head and neck cancer, but its role is best understood as **complementary rather than replacement** for conventional imaging. Across the branch reports, PET/CT is repeatedly described as improving tumor-volume delineation, changing radiotherapy planning decisions, influencing staging and prognosis, and being embedded in a complex workflow with important limitations and practical barriers. Below is a synthesis of the evidence across accuracy, treatment planning, and prognosis, with a final discussion of how PET/CT should be used in practice.

---

## 1) Accuracy of PET/CT for tumor volume delineation

### Main evidence base
The evidence supports PET/CT as a more accurate imaging modality than PET alone and as a useful tool for improving tumor-volume delineation in head and neck cancer [N1-F1][N4-R5][N4-F2]. The key metrics used to assess PET/CT accuracy are **sensitivity** and **specificity**, with the evidence reporting that PET outperforms CT in some staging comparisons [N1-F1]. It also states that PET/CT improves diagnostic accuracy and reduces false-positive results compared with standard PET alone [N1-R2].

### How PET/CT compares with CT or MRI
PET/CT is not universally superior to CT and MRI, but it adds value in specific contexts where anatomical imaging alone is limited. The evidence notes that CT and MRI are often used for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging because of their high spatial resolution and tissue contrast [N4-F2]. However, PET/CT is described as more accurate than PET alone in detection and anatomic localization of head and neck cancer [N4-R5].

For the primary tumor, the evidence states that PET can be at least as sensitive as CT/MRI in detecting the primary tumor, and in some studies has shown higher sensitivity, particularly for small or submucosal malignancies [N1-F1]. In oral cavity cancer, PET/CT had 96.3% detection performance versus 77.8% for CT and 85.2% for MRI [N1-F1]. The evidence also notes that PET/CT can refine GTV/PTV/CTV definitions and improve target-volume delineation, but that tumor boundaries can differ significantly across imaging modalities [N2-F3].

### Study populations and cancer subtypes
The evidence base is strongest for **head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)**, with the overview stating that most PET/CT applications in head and neck cancer are related to HNSCC [N1-F1]. It also specifically addresses **oral cavity cancer** and **oropharyngeal cancer**, and notes that **laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma** and other HNSCC subtypes are included in the evidence [N1-F1][N3-F4]. The PET/MRI comparison evidence refers to head and neck cancer gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation, indicating broad coverage of squamous cell malignancies and their anatomical variants [N1-R3].

### Bottom line on accuracy
PET/CT improves tumor-volume delineation and can outperform PET alone, but its accuracy depends on the clinical context. It is particularly valuable for detecting metastatic disease, submucosal tumors, and improving target-volume boundaries where anatomical imaging alone may be limited. However, it does not universally replace CT and MRI, and contouring can differ significantly across modalities [N1-F1][N4-F2][N2-F3].

---

## 2) Impact on treatment planning

### Whether PET/CT changes contouring decisions
Yes, PET/CT changes contouring decisions in radiotherapy planning. The evidence explicitly states that PET/CT can change GTV, PTV, and CTV definitions because tumor boundaries differ across imaging modalities [N2-F3]. It also says that PET/CT is used to provide accurate delineation of target volumes and treatment adaptation [N4-F2]. PET-based radiotherapy planning is described as useful for identifying viable tumor, necrotic areas, and locoregional metastatic lymph nodes, which directly informs contouring [N2-F3].

### Clinical outcomes linked to PET/CT-guided planning
The evidence links PET/CT-guided planning to improved clinical outcomes. It states that PET/CT can prevent unnecessary neck dissections when performed after chemoradiotherapy because of its high negative predictive value [N4-F2]. It also notes that PET/CT can improve primary tumor PTV coverage in some patients [N6-R4], and that PET/CT can alter treatment strategies, including surgical, radiation, and systemic treatment plans [N3-F4]. In staging, PET/CT can change the T, N, or M stage in almost half of patients, with the biggest impact being detection of additional nodal metastases and changing baseline management decisions [N3-F4].

### Trade-offs between contouring precision and clinical feasibility
The evidence identifies important trade-offs. PET/CT improves contouring precision, but it also introduces workflow complexity, requires coordination and teamwork, and is not a simple add-on step in the planning process [N2-F3]. The evidence also notes that PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results, and that its reliability can be affected by patient-related factors such as postoperative edema or renal function [N5-R4][N5-R2]. It further states that PET/CT is not always preferred for local staging of all newly diagnosed HNSCC because MRI and contrast-enhanced multislice CT have higher anatomic resolution [N1-F1]. These trade-offs imply that PET/CT should be used selectively rather than routinely in every patient.

### Bottom line on treatment planning
PET/CT changes contouring decisions and can improve clinical outcomes, particularly by preventing unnecessary dissections and refining target-volume definitions. However, it comes with workflow complexity and practical limitations, so its use must be balanced against anatomic imaging and clinical context [N2-F3][N4-F2][N6-R4].

---

## 3) Prognostic value and staging impact

### Prognostic variables associated with PET/CT findings
The evidence identifies several prognostic variables linked to PET/CT findings:
- **Maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax)**, which the evidence states is a potential prognostic marker for oropharyngeal cancer [N3-R5].
- **Metastatic disease detection**, because PET/CT can detect nodal and distant metastases and alter staging [N3-F4].
- **PET/CT-based parameters** that predict overall survival (OS) and distant metastasis-free survival in a multicenter study [N3-R3].
- **PET/CT findings at treatment response assessment**, which have high negative predictive value and can provide valuable prognostic implications [N3-R2].
- **PET/CT follow-up**, which may confer survival benefit compared with conventional follow-up in head and neck cancer [N3-R4].

### How PET/CT affects staging decisions and subsequent management
PET/CT changes staging decisions by changing the T, N, or M stage in almost half of patients, especially by detecting additional nodal metastases [N3-F4]. It is also described as useful for detecting occult primary tumors, synchronous second primaries, and distant metastases, all of which can change the initial staging and management plan [N1-F1][N3-F4]. PET/CT findings can lead to treatment plan alterations both in surgical and primary or adjuvant chemoradiation plans [N3-F4]. It can also guide treatment adaptation and avoid unnecessary neck dissections when performed after chemoradiotherapy [N4-F2].

### Whether PET/CT prognostic value is independent of conventional staging
The evidence suggests that PET/CT prognostic value is generally **additional** to conventional staging rather than independent of it. PET/CT is described as a complementary role to clinical evaluation and conventional imaging techniques, providing added advantage in the detection of synchronous and occult primary tumors and improving staging [N3-F4]. It is also noted that conventional imaging techniques are still used for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging, with PET/CT being preferred in certain scenarios such as detecting nodal involvement and distant metastases [N4-F2]. The evidence further emphasizes that PET/CT can predict outcomes at baseline and during or after treatment, but this is framed as an added layer of information rather than a replacement for conventional staging [N3-F4].

### Bottom line on prognosis and staging
PET/CT improves prognosis and staging by detecting metastases, occult primaries, and disease progression, and by changing treatment decisions. Its prognostic value is usually additional to conventional staging rather than entirely independent of it [N3-F4][N4-F2][N3-R3].

---

## 4) Workflow, guidelines, and practical use

### How PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy workflow
PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy planning as a complementary tool for target-volume delineation and treatment adaptation [N2-F3][N4-F2]. The evidence states that PET/CT provides 3D information regarding tumor volume and dose needed to irradiate the disease, and that PET-based radiotherapy planning is used in conjunction with image-guided RT and IMRT [N2-F3]. PET-defined biological tumor volume (BTV) can be used to determine radiation dose escalation [N2-F3]. Overall, PET/CT contouring is embedded within a broader treatment-planning pipeline rather than being a standalone step.

### Guidelines or consensus recommendations for PET/CT use
The evidence supports PET/CT in specific clinical scenarios and in advanced-stage disease. It states that PET/CT is recommended in patients with metastatic cervical lymphadenectomy and occult primary tumor, and that it is a well-established imaging tool for detecting cervical nodal involvement, distant metastases, and synchronous primary tumors [N4-F2]. It also notes that NCCN guidelines support the use of 18F-FDG PET/CT in advanced-stage disease in different clinical settings [N4-F2]. The 2025 Danish Head and Neck Cancer group guidelines further state that whole-body PET-CT scans can be used to detect distant metastasis or other primaries, and that 3D imaging below the clavicles may be used when appropriate [N6-R3].

### Practical barriers to adoption and routine use
Several practical barriers limit routine adoption. PET/CT-based planning is workflow-intensive and requires prior preparation, coordination, and teamwork in a PET center [N2-F3]. PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results, which can complicate interpretation and lead to unnecessary interventions [N5-R2][N5-R4]. It is also noted that PET/CT is not always preferred for local staging of all newly diagnosed HNSCC, because MRI and contrast-enhanced multislice CT have higher anatomic resolution [N1-F1]. Patient-related factors such as postoperative edema or renal function can reduce reliability [N2-F3]. Finally, the evidence warns that early PET/CT after treatment can have significant false-positive rates and is not recommended in the absence of signs of disease [N5-R2].

### Bottom line on workflow and practical use
PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy workflow as a complementary tool, but its adoption is limited by workflow complexity, false-positive/false-negative risks, and patient-related limitations. It is supported in specific clinical scenarios and advanced-stage disease, but routine use should be selective [N2-F3][N4-F2][N5-R2][N6-R3].

---

## 5) Broader context and limitations

### Main limitations
The evidence identifies several main limitations of PET/CT in head and neck cancer:
- **Motion and fusion quality**: PET/CT is more accurate than PET alone in detection and anatomic localization, but it still depends on accurate fusion and localization [N4-R5].
- **Partial volume effects and heterogeneity**: PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results, and can miss microscopic metastases or nodal metastases close to normal structures [N5-R1][N5-R4].
- **Heterogeneity of tumor biology**: PET/CT is limited by the fact that tumor boundaries and uptake patterns can differ significantly across imaging modalities [N2-F3][N1-F1].

### How patient selection affects reliability
Patient selection strongly affects PET/CT reliability. The evidence notes that PET/CT can be less reliable in patients with postoperative edema, because tumor margins may become confounded [N2-F3]. It also notes that PET/CT can be affected by patient-related issues such as high serum creatinine or post-renal transplant status, where contrast-enhanced CT may not be feasible [N2-F3]. In addition, early PET/CT after treatment is associated with significant false-positive rates and is not recommended in the absence of signs of disease [N5-R2].

### Overuse or underuse
The evidence suggests both overuse and underuse concerns. On one hand, PET/CT is described as having a well-established role in pre-treatment staging, radiotherapy planning, treatment-response assessment, and post-therapy follow-up [N4-F2]. On the other hand, it warns against overuse in all patients, because early PET/CT after treatment can have significant false-positive rates [N5-R2]. It also suggests underuse concerns when clinicians rely too heavily on conventional imaging and do not incorporate PET/CT appropriately into follow-up and staging workflows [N3-R4][N4-F2].

### Bottom line on broader context
PET/CT has important limitations, including motion, partial volume effects, and heterogeneity. Its reliability depends on patient selection and clinical context, and the evidence suggests that PET/CT should be used selectively rather than overused in all patients. It can be underused if clinicians do not incorporate it appropriately into follow-up and staging workflows [N4-R5][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-F3].

---

## 6) Overall conclusion

### What the evidence supports
- **Accuracy**: PET/CT improves tumor-volume delineation and is more accurate than PET alone, but not universally superior to CT and MRI [N1-F1][N4-R5][N4-F2].
- **Treatment planning**: PET/CT changes contouring decisions, can improve clinical outcomes, and can prevent unnecessary dissections [N2-F3][N4-F2][N6-R4].
- **Prognosis and staging**: PET/CT is associated with prognostic variables such as SUVmax, metastatic disease, and treatment response; it changes staging decisions and treatment management [N3-R5][N3-F4][N3-R3].
- **Workflow and guidelines**: PET/CT is integrated into radiotherapy workflow and supported in specific clinical scenarios, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity and practical barriers [N2-F3][N4-F2][N6-R3].

### What the evidence does **not** support
- Universal replacement of CT and MRI for all staging and contouring tasks.
- Routine overuse of PET/CT in every patient or setting.
- Independent prognostic value of PET/CT that is completely separate from conventional staging [N3-F4][N4-F2].

### Practical recommendation
PET/CT should be used as a **complementary, context-sensitive tool** in head and neck cancer. It is especially valuable for detecting metastases, refining target volumes, and improving staging in advanced disease, but its use should be guided by clinical context, patient selection, and the need to balance precision with feasibility [N1-F1][N4-F2][N2-F3][N5-R2].

The evidence supports PET/CT as a tool that improves tumor-volume delineation in head and neck cancer, especially for identifying metastatic disease and refining target-volume boundaries where anatomical imaging alone is limited. ### Imaging metrics used to assess PET/CT accuracy
The evidence repeatedly cites sensitivity and specificity as the main metrics used to assess PET/CT performance. For example, it states that literature comparing 18F-FDG PET to CT indicates PET has higher sensitivity (87% versus 62%) and higher specificity (89% versus 73%) for staging cancer [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that PET/CT improves diagnostic accuracy and reduces false-positive results compared with standard PET alone [N1-R2]. In the broader discussion, PET/CT is described as providing better localization and enabling more accurate delineation of tumor volume and treatment adaptation [N4-F2]. These metrics are therefore central to the evidence base for PET/CT accuracy.

### How PET/CT compares with CT or MRI for gross tumor volume definition
PET/CT is presented as superior to CT and MRI in some key scenarios, but not universally superior for all aspects of delineation. The evidence says that CT and MRI are often used for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging, and that they can be preferred in certain contexts because of their high spatial resolution and tissue contrast [N4-F2]. However, PET/CT is described as more accurate than PET alone in detection and anatomic localization of head and neck cancer [N4-R5]. For the primary tumor, the evidence notes that PET can be at least as sensitive as CT/MRI in detecting the primary tumor, and in some studies has shown higher sensitivity, particularly for small or submucosal malignancies [N1-F1]. In oral cavity cancer, PET/CT had 96.3% detection performance versus 77.8% for CT and 85.2% for MRI [N1-F1].

The evidence also states that PET/CT is used to provide accurate delineation of target volumes and treatment adaptation for radiation therapy planning [N4-F2]. It further notes that PET-based software provides 3D information regarding tumor volume and dose needed to irradiate the disease, which suggests that PET/CT can refine GTV contours by incorporating functional information about viable tumor and necrotic areas [N2-F3]. However, the same evidence also warns that PET-based contouring can differ significantly from CT or MRI-based contours, because the boundaries of primary tumors can differ across modalities [N2-F3].

The evidence supports PET/CT as more accurate than PET alone and as useful for improving tumor-volume delineation in head and neck cancer, especially for primary tumors and nodal metastases. ## Evidence on treatment planning impact

The evidence indicates that PET/CT can change contouring decisions in radiotherapy planning and can improve clinical outcomes, but it also notes practical trade-offs between precision and feasibility.

### Whether PET/CT changes contouring decisions in radiotherapy planning
Yes, PET/CT changes contouring decisions. The evidence explicitly states that PET/CT can change the GTV, planning target volume (PTV), and clinical target volume (CTV) because tumor boundaries differ across imaging modalities [N2-F3]. It also says that PET/CT is used to provide accurate delineation of target volumes and treatment adaptation [N4-F2]. In a practical workflow context, PET/CT is described as useful for identifying viable tumor, its margins, necrotic areas, and locoregional metastatic lymph nodes, which directly informs contouring [N2-F3]. In addition, PET/CT can lead to changes in nodal status and/or detection of distant metastasis, which can alter treatment planning [N2-F3].

The evidence further indicates that PET-based radiotherapy planning can improve primary tumor PTV coverage. In one study cited in the evidence, PET/CT-based planning improved primary tumor PTV coverage in 37.2% of cases [N6-R4]. This implies that PET/CT can change contouring decisions by expanding or tightening GTV/PTV definitions in a clinically meaningful way.

### Clinical outcomes linked to PET/CT-guided planning
The evidence links PET/CT-guided planning to improved clinical outcomes. In the precision radiotherapy review, PET/CT is said to hold promise for better clinical outcomes and is described as exciting and potentially useful for management of head and neck cancers with better clinical outcomes [N2-F3]. It also notes that PET/CT can prevent unnecessary neck dissections when performed after chemoradiotherapy, because of its high negative predictive value [N4-F2]. This indicates that PET/CT can avoid overtreatment and reduce morbidity.

The evidence also suggests that PET/CT can alter treatment strategies, including surgical, radiation, and systemic treatment plans, because PET/CT findings can change staging [N3-F4]. In the staging context, the evidence states that PET/CT can change the T, N, or M stages in almost half the patients, with the biggest impact being in the detection of additional nodal metastases and changing baseline management decisions [N3-F4]. This has direct consequences for treatment planning.

### Trade-offs between contouring precision and clinical feasibility
The evidence highlights important trade-offs. One major trade-off is that PET/CT improves contouring precision, but it also introduces complexity. The evidence notes that GTV boundaries can differ significantly between PET, CT, and MRI, and that this can affect the choice of anatomic boundaries when high doses are delivered to lesions close to radiosensitive structures [N2-F3]. It also emphasizes that PET/CT-based planning requires prior preparation, coordination, and teamwork in a PET center, which implies workflow complexity [N2-F3].

Another trade-off is between precision and practicality. The evidence states that CT and MRI are often preferred for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging because of their high spatial resolution and tissue contrast, even though PET/CT can be superior in certain contexts [N4-F2]. It also notes that PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results, and that its reliability can be affected by patient-related factors such as postoperative edema or renal function [N5-R4][N5-R2]. These limitations suggest that PET/CT should be used judiciously rather than routinely in all patients, because its added value depends on clinical context.

### Bottom line
PET/CT changes contouring decisions in radiotherapy planning by refining GTV/PTV/CTV definitions and altering treatment strategies. The evidence associates PET/CT-guided planning with improved clinical outcomes, including prevention of unnecessary dissections and better treatment adaptation. However, precision comes with trade-offs: contouring can differ across modalities, workflow complexity increases, and PET/CT is not a perfect substitute for anatomical imaging in every clinical situation [N2-F3][N4-F2][N6-R4].

## Broader context and limitations of PET/CT use

The evidence identifies several main limitations, patient-selection effects, and concerns about overuse or underuse of PET/CT in head and neck cancer.

### Main limitations such as motion, partial volume effects, and heterogeneity
PET/CT is limited by several technical and biological factors. First, the evidence notes that PET/CT is more accurate than PET alone in detection and anatomic localization, but it still depends on accurate fusion and localization [N4-R5]. The evidence also explicitly states that PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results [N5-R2][N5-R4]. In addition, the evidence mentions that false-negative findings can occur when the primary tumor is superficial or small (T1 tumors) and that PET/CT can miss microscopic metastases or nodal metastases close to normal structures [N5-R1][N5-R4]. These limitations reflect the challenge of partial volume effects and the heterogeneity of tumor biology.

The evidence also highlights that PET/CT is limited by motion artifacts and by the need for accurate fusion with anatomical CT. It states that PET alone has limitations with respect to lesion localization, and that PET/CT overcomes this limitation by combining metabolic and anatomic information [N1-F1]. This implies that motion and fusion quality remain important practical limitations.

### How patient selection affects PET/CT reliability
Patient selection significantly affects PET/CT reliability. The evidence notes that PET/CT can be less reliable in patients with postoperative edema, because tumor margins may become confounded [N2-F3]. It also notes that PET/CT can be affected by patient-related issues such as high serum creatinine or post-renal transplant status, where contrast-enhanced CT may not be feasible [N2-F3]. In addition, the evidence states that PET/CT is not recommended in the absence of signs of disease when early PET/CT is performed 3 months after the end of radiotherapy, because of significant false-positive rates [N5-R2]. These examples show that PET/CT reliability depends on clinical context, tumor biology, and patient factors.

The evidence further indicates that PET/CT is not universally preferred for local staging of all newly diagnosed HNSCC, because MRI and contrast-enhanced multislice CT have higher anatomic resolution [N1-F1]. This suggests that PET/CT should be used selectively rather than routinely for every patient.

### What the evidence says about overuse or underuse of PET/CT
The evidence indicates both overuse and underuse concerns. On the one hand, PET/CT is described as having a well-established role in pre-treatment staging, radiotherapy planning, treatment-response assessment, and post-therapy follow-up [N4-F2]. However, it also warns that PET/CT should not be overused in all patients. The evidence specifically states that early PET/CT, 3 months after the end of radiotherapy, is associated with significant false-positive rates and is not recommended in the absence of signs of disease [N5-R2]. Similarly, the evidence cautions that PET/CT is not the first-line imaging modality for every clinical scenario, because CT and MRI are often preferred for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging [N4-F2].

The evidence also suggests underuse concerns in some settings. For example, it states that PET/CT is valuable in detecting recurrences and metastases during follow-up when suspected because of clinical symptoms, and that it serves as a prognostic marker [N3-R2]. It also notes that PET/CT can be used for follow-up and may confer survival benefit compared with conventional follow-up [N3-R4]. These findings suggest that PET/CT can be underused in routine follow-up if clinicians rely too heavily on conventional imaging.

### Bottom line
PET/CT has important limitations, including motion, partial volume effects, heterogeneity, and the potential for false-positive and false-negative findings. Patient selection strongly affects reliability, especially in postoperative, renal, or small-tumor settings. The evidence suggests that PET/CT should be used selectively rather than overused in all patients, and that it can be underused if clinicians do not incorporate it appropriately into follow-up and staging workflows [N4-R5][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-F3][N4-F2].

PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy planning through a coordinated workflow that combines PET with anatomical CT. It also says that PET-based radiotherapy planning requires prior preparation, coordination, and teamwork in a PET center [N2-F3]. The evidence includes some guideline-like statements. The 2025 Danish Head and Neck Cancer group guidelines state that whole-body PET-CT scans can be used to detect distant metastasis or other primaries, and that 3D imaging below the clavicles may be used when appropriate [N6-R3]. Several practical barriers limit routine use. First, PET/CT-based planning is workflow-intensive and requires coordination, teamwork, and prior preparation [N2-F3]. ### Bottom line
PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy workflow as a complementary tool for target-volume delineation and treatment adaptation, but it is not a simple add-on step. The evidence supports its use in specific clinical scenarios and in advanced-stage disease, but practical barriers such as workflow complexity, false-positive/false-negative risks, and patient-related limitations make routine adoption challenging [N2-F3][N4-F2][N5-R2][N5-R4][N6-R3].

### Bottom line on treatment planning
PET/CT changes contouring decisions and can improve clinical outcomes, particularly by preventing unnecessary dissections and refining target-volume definitions. However, it comes with workflow complexity and practical limitations, so its use must be balanced against anatomic imaging and clinical context [N2-F3][N4-F2][N6-R4].

## 3) Prognostic value and staging impact

### Prognostic variables associated with PET/CT findings
The evidence identifies several prognostic variables linked to PET/CT findings:
- **Maximum standardized uptake value (SUVmax)**, which the evidence states is a potential prognostic marker for oropharyngeal cancer [N3-R5].
- **Metastatic disease detection**, because PET/CT can detect nodal and distant metastases and alter staging [N3-F4].
- **PET/CT-based parameters** that predict overall survival (OS) and distant metastasis-free survival in a multicenter study [N3-R3].
- **PET/CT findings at treatment response assessment**, which have high negative predictive value and can provide valuable prognostic implications [N3-R2].
- **PET/CT follow-up**, which may confer survival benefit compared with conventional follow-up in head and neck cancer [N3-R4].

### How PET/CT affects staging decisions and subsequent management
PET/CT changes staging decisions by changing the T, N, or M stage in almost half of patients, especially by detecting additional nodal metastases [N3-F4]. It is also described as useful for detecting occult primary tumors, synchronous second primaries, and distant metastases, all of which can change the initial staging and management plan [N1-F1][N3-F4]. PET/CT findings can lead to treatment plan alterations both in surgical and primary or adjuvant chemoradiation plans [N3-F4]. It can also guide treatment adaptation and avoid unnecessary neck dissections when performed after chemoradiotherapy [N4-F2].

### Whether PET/CT prognostic value is independent of conventional staging
The evidence suggests that PET/CT prognostic value is generally **additional** to conventional staging rather than independent of it. PET/CT is described as a complementary role to clinical evaluation and conventional imaging techniques, providing added advantage in the detection of synchronous and occult primary tumors and improving staging [N3-F4]. It is also noted that conventional imaging techniques are still used for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging, with PET/CT being preferred in certain scenarios such as detecting nodal involvement and distant metastases [N4-F2]. The evidence further emphasizes that PET/CT can predict outcomes at baseline and during or after treatment, but this is framed as an added layer of information rather than a replacement for conventional staging [N3-F4].

### Bottom line on prognosis and staging
PET/CT improves prognosis and staging by detecting metastases, occult primaries, and disease progression, and by changing treatment decisions. Its prognostic value is usually additional to conventional staging rather than entirely independent of it [N3-F4][N4-F2][N3-R3].

## 4) Workflow, guidelines, and practical use

### How PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy workflow
PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy planning as a complementary tool for target-volume delineation and treatment adaptation [N2-F3][N4-F2]. The evidence states that PET/CT provides 3D information regarding tumor volume and dose needed to irradiate the disease, and that PET-based radiotherapy planning is used in conjunction with image-guided RT and IMRT [N2-F3]. PET-defined biological tumor volume (BTV) can be used to determine radiation dose escalation [N2-F3]. The evidence supports PET/CT in specific clinical scenarios and in advanced-stage disease. It states that PET/CT is recommended in patients with metastatic cervical lymphadenectomy and occult primary tumor, and that it is a well-established imaging tool for detecting cervical nodal involvement, distant metastases, and synchronous primary tumors [N4-F2]. It also notes that NCCN guidelines support the use of 18F-FDG PET/CT in advanced-stage disease in different clinical settings [N4-F2]. The 2025 Danish Head and Neck Cancer group guidelines further state that whole-body PET-CT scans can be used to detect distant metastasis or other primaries, and that 3D imaging below the clavicles may be used when appropriate [N6-R3].

### Practical barriers to adoption and routine use
Several practical barriers limit routine adoption. PET/CT-based planning is workflow-intensive and requires prior preparation, coordination, and teamwork in a PET center [N2-F3]. PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results, which can complicate interpretation and lead to unnecessary interventions [N5-R2][N5-R4]. It is also noted that PET/CT is not always preferred for local staging of all newly diagnosed HNSCC, because MRI and contrast-enhanced multislice CT have higher anatomic resolution [N1-F1]. Patient-related factors such as postoperative edema or renal function can reduce reliability [N2-F3]. Finally, the evidence warns that early PET/CT after treatment can have significant false-positive rates and is not recommended in the absence of signs of disease [N5-R2].

### Bottom line on workflow and practical use
PET/CT contouring is integrated into radiotherapy workflow as a complementary tool, but its adoption is limited by workflow complexity, false-positive/false-negative risks, and patient-related limitations. It is supported in specific clinical scenarios and advanced-stage disease, but routine use should be selective [N2-F3][N4-F2][N5-R2][N6-R3].

---

## 5) Broader context and limitations

### Main limitations
The evidence identifies several main limitations of PET/CT in head and neck cancer:
- **Motion and fusion quality**: PET/CT is more accurate than PET alone in detection and anatomic localization, but it still depends on accurate fusion and localization [N4-R5].
- **Partial volume effects and heterogeneity**: PET/CT can produce false-positive and false-negative results, and can miss microscopic metastases or nodal metastases close to normal structures [N5-R1][N5-R4].
- **Heterogeneity of tumor biology**: PET/CT is limited by the fact that tumor boundaries and uptake patterns can differ significantly across imaging modalities [N2-F3][N1-F1].

### How patient selection affects reliability
Patient selection strongly affects PET/CT reliability. The evidence notes that PET/CT can be less reliable in patients with postoperative edema, because tumor margins may become confounded [N2-F3]. It also notes that PET/CT can be affected by patient-related issues such as high serum creatinine or post-renal transplant status, where contrast-enhanced CT may not be feasible [N2-F3]. In addition, early PET/CT after treatment is associated with significant false-positive rates and is not recommended in the absence of signs of disease [N5-R2].

### Overuse or underuse
The evidence suggests both overuse and underuse concerns. On one hand, PET/CT is described as having a well-established role in pre-treatment staging, radiotherapy planning, treatment-response assessment, and post-therapy follow-up [N4-F2]. On the other hand, it warns against overuse in all patients, because early PET/CT after treatment can have significant false-positive rates [N5-R2]. It also suggests underuse concerns when clinicians rely too heavily on conventional imaging and do not incorporate PET/CT appropriately into follow-up and staging workflows [N3-R4][N4-F2].

### Bottom line on broader context
PET/CT has important limitations, including motion, partial volume effects, and heterogeneity. Its reliability depends on patient selection and clinical context, and the evidence suggests that PET/CT should be used selectively rather than overused in all patients. It can be underused if clinicians do not incorporate it appropriately into follow-up and staging workflows [N4-R5][N5-R1][N5-R2][N2-F3].

---

## 6) Overall conclusion

### What the evidence supports
- **Accuracy**: PET/CT improves tumor-volume delineation and is more accurate than PET alone, but not universally superior to CT and MRI [N1-F1][N4-R5][N4-F2].
- **Treatment planning**: PET/CT changes contouring decisions, can improve clinical outcomes, and can prevent unnecessary dissections [N2-F3][N4-F2][N6-R4].
- **Prognosis and staging**: PET/CT is associated with prognostic variables such as SUVmax, metastatic disease, and treatment response; it changes staging decisions and treatment management [N3-R5][N3-F4][N3-R3].
- **Workflow and guidelines**: PET/CT is integrated into radiotherapy workflow and supported in specific clinical scenarios, but adoption is limited by workflow complexity and practical barriers [N2-F3][N4-F2][N6-R3].

### What the evidence does **not** support
- Universal replacement of CT and MRI for all staging and contouring tasks.
- Routine overuse of PET/CT in every patient or setting.
- Independent prognostic value of PET/CT that is completely separate from conventional staging [N3-F4][N4-F2].

### Practical recommendation
PET/CT should be used as a **complementary, context-sensitive tool** in head and neck cancer. It is especially valuable for detecting metastases, refining target volumes, and improving staging in advanced disease, but its use should be guided by clinical context, patient selection, and the need to balance precision with feasibility [N1-F1][N4-F2][N2-F3][N5-R2].

### Imaging metrics used to assess PET/CT accuracy
The evidence repeatedly cites sensitivity and specificity as the main metrics used to assess PET/CT performance. For example, it states that literature comparing 18F-FDG PET to CT indicates PET has higher sensitivity (87% versus 62%) and higher specificity (89% versus 73%) for staging cancer [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that PET/CT improves diagnostic accuracy and reduces false-positive results compared with standard PET alone [N1-R2]. However, PET/CT is described as more accurate than PET alone in detection and anatomic localization of head and neck cancer [N4-R5]. For the primary tumor, the evidence notes that PET can be at least as sensitive as CT/MRI in detecting the primary tumor, and in some studies has shown higher sensitivity, particularly for small or submucosal malignancies [N1-F1]. The evidence base covers a broad range of head and neck cancer subtypes, with the strongest emphasis on **head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)**. The evidence supports PET/CT as more accurate than PET alone and as useful for improving tumor-volume delineation in head and neck cancer, especially for primary tumors and nodal metastases. ## Evidence on PET/CT accuracy for tumor volume delineation

The evidence supports PET/CT as a tool that improves tumor-volume delineation in head and neck cancer, especially for identifying metastatic disease and refining target-volume boundaries where anatomical imaging alone is limited. The accuracy discussion in the evidence is centered on sensitivity, specificity, and whether PET/CT adds value over CT or MRI for detecting disease and defining gross tumor volume (GTV) boundaries.

### Imaging metrics used to assess PET/CT accuracy
The evidence repeatedly cites sensitivity and specificity as the main metrics used to assess PET/CT performance. For example, it states that literature comparing 18F-FDG PET to CT indicates PET has higher sensitivity (87% versus 62%) and higher specificity (89% versus 73%) for staging cancer [N1-F1]. It also emphasizes that PET/CT improves diagnostic accuracy and reduces false-positive results compared with standard PET alone [N1-R2]. In the broader discussion, PET/CT is described as providing better localization and enabling more accurate delineation of tumor volume and treatment adaptation [N4-F2]. These metrics are therefore central to the evidence base for PET/CT accuracy.

### How PET/CT compares with CT or MRI for gross tumor volume definition
PET/CT is presented as superior to CT and MRI in some key scenarios, but not universally superior for all aspects of delineation. The evidence says that CT and MRI are often used for primary tumor evaluation and loco-regional staging, and that they can be preferred in certain contexts because of their high spatial resolution and tissue contrast [N4-F2]. However, PET/CT is described as more accurate than PET alone in detection and anatomic localization of head and neck cancer [N4-R5]. For the primary tumor, the evidence notes that PET can be at least as sensitive as CT/MRI in detecting the primary tumor, and in some studies has shown higher sensitivity, particularly for small or submucosal malignancies [N1-F1]. In oral cavity cancer, PET/CT had 96.3% detection performance versus 77.8% for CT and 85.2% for MRI [N1-F1].

The evidence also states that PET/CT is used to provide accurate delineation of target volumes and treatment adaptation for radiation therapy planning [N4-F2]. It further notes that PET-based software provides 3D information regarding tumor volume and dose needed to irradiate the disease, which suggests that PET/CT can refine GTV contours by incorporating functional information about viable tumor and necrotic areas [N2-F3]. However, the same evidence also warns that PET-based contouring can differ significantly from CT or MRI-based contours, because the boundaries of primary tumors can differ across modalities [N2-F3].

### Study populations and cancer subtypes covered in the evidence
The evidence base covers a broad range of head and neck cancer subtypes, with the strongest emphasis on **head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC)**. The overview explicitly states that most PET/CT applications in head and neck cancer are related to HNSCC [N1-F1]. It also specifically addresses **oral cavity cancer**, where PET/CT showed higher sensitivity than CT and MRI [N1-F1]. The evidence also touches on **oropharyngeal cancer**, **laryngeal squamous cell carcinoma**, and other HNSCC subtypes, and notes that HPV status and p16 status are important variables in prognosis and treatment decisions [N3-F4]. In the PET/MRI comparison, the evidence refers to head and neck cancer gross tumor volume (GTV) delineation, indicating that the subtype focus is broad but centered on squamous cell malignancies and their anatomical variants [N1-R3]. Overall, the evidence is strongest for HNSCC and its subtypes, with some support for broader head and neck tumor types [N4-F2].

### Bottom line
The evidence supports PET/CT as more accurate than PET alone and as useful for improving tumor-volume delineation in head and neck cancer, especially for primary tumors and nodal metastases. However, it does not claim universal superiority over CT and MRI; rather, it suggests that PET/CT adds value in specific contexts where anatomical imaging alone is limited, and that contouring decisions can differ across modalities [N1-F1][N4-F2][N2-F3].
